new_statements.quote: Подводя итоги, можно сделать вывод о том, что смыслоразличительного ударения в лесном ненецком говоре с. Халясавей нет. Выше можно увидеть достаточно много примеров, когда максимальная интенсивность и длительность маркируют разные слоги в словоформе. [...] В большинстве случаев максимальная интенсивность маркирует гласный первого слога, исключения составляют слова с кратким ĭ в первом слоге и примерно половина слов с кратким ŭ. А максимальная длительность в большинстве случаев, наоборот, маркирует открытый гласный второго слога.
new_statements.translation: Summing up, one can conclude that there is no distinctive (phonemic) stress in the Forest Nenets dialect of the village of Khalyasavey. Above one can see quite a few examples where maximal intensity and maximal duration mark different syllables of a word form. [...] In most cases maximal intensity marks the vowel of the first syllable; the exceptions are words with a short ĭ in the first syllable and about half of the words with a short ŭ. Maximal duration, by contrast, in most cases marks the open vowel of the second syllable. (English abstract, p. 184: 'suggesting the absence of classical stress in contemporary Forest Nenets ... Generally, the vowel in the initial syllable is characterized by the maximum intensity, with the exception of words containing a short ĭ in the first syllable and about half of the words containing a short ŭ.')

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has Forest Nenets with an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this is new information rather than agreement or contradiction. Dialect-specific (Khalyasavey village, Pur district); it explicitly disagrees with the placement rules reported secondhand for Sammallahti 1974 (weight-sensitive initial/second) and Burkova 2022: 681 (initial or non-initial closed syllable), e.g. for pîja 'nose' Sammallahti would predict second-syllable stress and Burkova first-syllable (p. 185).
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Khalyasavey dialect there is no phonologically distinctive word stress: intensity peak and duration peak often fall on different syllables and can shift between two pronunciations of the same word by the same speaker. Phonetically, the intensity peak is on the first syllable in most words (except words with short ĭ, and about half of those with short ŭ, in the first syllable, where a non-initial syllable often carries the intensity peak), while the duration peak usually falls on an open second-syllable vowel. The author attributes the initial intensity peak to an areal process (also Gydan Tundra Nenets per Amelina, Surgut Khanty, Tundra Enets, Taz Selkup).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for the author's own data. Literature review p. 185 paraphrases Sammallahti 1974: 29-31 (one speaker, outside the home area): main stress as a rule on the first syllable, but if the first syllable is short and the second long, stress moves to the second syllable; secondary stress on the third, fifth and following syllables, and a closed second syllable receives secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with short ĭ in the first syllable and about half of the words with short ŭ in the first syllable have the intensity peak on a non-initial syllable (reflexes of Proto-Nenets short *i, *u vs long *ī, *ū). Popova 1978's dictionary marks variable ('разноместное') stress, which the author's data do not support as phonological; Lehtisalo 1956 marks length in places that do not match Popova's stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Normanskaja 2025 describes the Khalyasavey village dialect of Forest Nenets (recordings from 2012) and states the result for that dialect; the the Harvard library catalogue-indexed item behind the listed open_url is a Tundra Nenets (tund1255) article, not Forest Nenets. Burkova 2022 covers both Tundra and Forest Nenets in one chapter; the secondhand p.681 statement is about 'the Nenets languages' generally.

readall_conflicts: The only work actually read (Normanskaja 2025, Khalyasavey dialect, instrumental) concludes there is no phonologically distinctive word stress, with a phonetic intensity peak on the first syllable in most words (exceptions: short ĭ/ŭ in the first syllable) and a duration peak usually on an open second syllable. The listed work (Burkova 2022: 681, not openable) is reported by Normanskaja (p. 185) as placing stress on the first syllable or a non-initial closed syllable, taken from earlier literature; Sammallahti 1974: 29-31 (paraphrased p. 185) gives initial stress that shifts to a long second syllable after a short first syllable, with secondary stress on odd syllables and on a closed second syllable; Popova 1978 marks variable stress in her dictionary. Normanskaja states these rules contradict each other (e.g. pîja 'nose': second-syllable stress by Sammallahti, first by Burkova and Popova). The common thread across all sources is initial-syllable prominence as the default; they differ on whether it is phonological and on the weight/closed-syllable conditions.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is present verbatim in the Salminen 2007 PDF we hold/text at pp.350, 357, 359 and 367 as cited. (2) Deciding source: a 2007 phonology article by the field's leading specialist; stress is stated as a by-product of the vowel-alternation analysis rather than in a dedicated section, but the rule (non-final odd syllables + pre-schwa syllables; schwa syllables unstressed) is explicit and is independently restated and endorsed by two held later sources (Burkova/IJaz RAN minlang page; Agicheva, Kozlov & Toldova 2026 fieldwork: 'confirms the validity of Salminen's system'). (3) New evidence downloaded now: Normanskaja 2025, the only instrumental study of Forest Nenets prominence, concludes there is no contrastive ('смыслоразличительное') stress, with intensity maxima mostly on the first syllable and duration maxima often on an open second syllab
